summary: Research deliverable landed: docs/research/cloudflare-platform-limits.md, 943 lines with 31 distinct cited official Cloudflare URLs and 11 explicitly unverified items. It resolves open question Q5 and materially narrows Q2/Q3/Q4. Key facts now locked as decisions D8-D13 in STATE.md: Workers inbound body is capped by the ZONE plan (Free/Pro 100 MB) while a Worker isolate has only 128 MB memory, so large-file ingest must be chunked; R2 multipart state must live outside the Worker (Cloudflare states this explicitly), making the chunk-session schema a day-one D1 decision; R2 multipart needs >=5 MiB parts, <=10000 parts, <=5 GiB per part, <=4.995 TiB per object, and allows only 1 write/sec per key; R2 egress is free and an R2 object body can be returned as the Response body with no enforced size limit; presigned URLs expire in 1s-7d, cannot use custom domains, and are unrevocable bearer tokens; D1 is documented as auto-commit with db.batch() as the only atomic unit and no BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK anywhere; D1 replicas may be arbitrarily out of date unless withSession()/bookmark is used; only 6 concurrent in-flight connections are allowed per invocation, shared across fetch/R2/D1/KV/Queues/Cache; Cron gives 5 triggers per account on Free with minute granularity, UTC only, and no documented delivery guarantee.

Corrected an earlier inaccurate environment claim. STATE.md and AGENTS.md previously implied the machine had no usable web access. The accurate fact is narrower: the harness web_fetch tool is rejected because public hostnames resolve to the non-public TUN address 198.18.0.203. Ordinary HTTP works, and fetching the .md variant of a docs page with Invoke-WebRequest is a proven, reproducible path. Both files were corrected so a future session does not wrongly conclude that primary-source research is impossible here.

Process incident, self-reported: a throwaway helper script (.scratch/vps-file-hub/tmp-record.ps1) was swept into commit 4ab3a17 by a broad git add -A and pushed to main without a predeclared operation event, because the commit that carried the research note also staged an unrelated temp file. Impact: one disposable 5 KB script is present in the public main history at 4ab3a17, which is not a secret leak (the only credential-keyword match is the technical term bearer tokens) but does violate the predeclaration discipline and adds an unintended file to a public repository. Correction: the file is removed in the following commit. Chosen remedy is a normal follow-up commit rather than a force-push rewrite of main, because rewriting already-published main history is a force operation that the current authorization does not cover and would break the default branch for anyone who has fetched it. Recorded so the residue in history is not mistaken for intentional content later.

Round 2-3 of grill-with-docs. The user rejected the previous collection model outright: nothing is installed on the VPS; instead the Worker itself reaches the hosts over SSH. The user knowingly accepted that this path cannot be verified locally, so a prototype gate was inserted before to-spec. Also locked: password-only SSH auth; credentials entered in the web UI and stored encrypted with the decryption key held as a Worker secret; a 25 MB chunking threshold with no compression; download-time password check only (real at-rest encryption deferred to its own ticket); the web UI hosted on the same Worker with a capped scope; single-file maximum size generally under 100 MB; Workers paid plan confirmed; test VPS will be provided by the user and is read-only for this work; prototype code lives on a prototype/ssh-probe branch that is never merged.

Research finding that invalidates part of the requested initialisation design: a running Worker cannot provision its own D1 database and R2 bucket and then bind to them, because bindings are deploy-time configuration and Cloudflare documents the D1 REST API as control-plane/administrative rather than a data-plane path. The documented in-Worker pattern is a proxy in front of an existing binding. The initialisation feature therefore has to stay outside the Worker as a CLI/CI step driven by CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN + CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID, which IS fully non-interactive. Only API-token creation and the R2 subscription checkout genuinely need a human at a browser. Recorded so no ticket promises Worker self-provisioning.

summary: The user was right and I was wrong: resources CAN be auto-provisioned at deploy time. I had asserted that D1 must be created beforehand and that database_id is required. Cloudflare documents an Automatic provisioning feature under which wrangler deploy creates KV, R2, D1 and others when the configuration declares a binding WITHOUT a resource id (and for R2, without a bucket name), naming them after the Worker. Behaviour differs by path: wrangler dev creates local resources that persist; wrangler deploy creates them and writes their ids back to the config file; but deploying from the dashboard (which is what Workers Builds does) creates the resources and does NOT write the ids back into the repository. wrangler.jsonc was rewritten accordingly to omit database_id and bucket_name. Recorded as decision D31.

Credential architecture specified by the user: only the key lives in the deployment secret, while each host address, port and credential is encrypted with that key and stored in D1, and arbitrary hosts plus their collection directory paths are added through the project front end. Implemented as: single SSH_MASTER_KEY secret; AES-GCM 256 via WebCrypto with a fresh random IV per encryption and the host id plus field name bound in as additional authenticated data; the API returns only a fingerprint, never a credential; hosts and source_rules tables added; global rules use a NULL host_id and per-host rules a host_id, unioned at collection time with exclusions evaluated first. Recorded as D32 and D33. An explicit honest limit is recorded rather than glossed over: an attacker holding both the D1 database and the master key can recover every credential.

summary: Prototype verdict: PASS. A deployed Worker connected to a real remote host over SSH and returned its bytes intact. Measured on the deployed Worker: ssh connect + auth 288-294 ms, sftp list /etc 202 ms (83 entries), sftp readFile 214 ms, WebCrypto sha256 under 1 ms, r2 put 217 ms; roughly 1.4 s end to end per file. Three files were checked against a hash computed independently ON THE HOST by sha256sum: /etc/hostname (24 bytes), /etc/alpine-release (7 bytes) and /etc/passwd (1226 bytes) all matched exactly, and the R2 objects were confirmed present with identical sizes. This closes the CPU-budget risk recorded as D24: the handshake uses about one hundredth of the paid plan ceiling, so the collection channel chosen in D14 is viable.

Bug found only against a real host, and the reason it could not be caught locally: Wrangler bundles without type checking, and edgeport AlgorithmPrefs.cipher is an ARRAY of algorithm names, but the code passed a bare string. The handshake therefore died at KEXINIT construction with TypeError names.join is not a function. Fixed by passing a preference list with AES-GCM first and aes-ctr as fallback; chacha20-poly1305 stays excluded because it would be pure JS. A list was chosen over a single pinned cipher so a host without GCM still works. The JSON error response now also carries a stack, because with no type checking in the build a dependency shape mistake can only surface at runtime and a stack turns that from guesswork into a line number.

summary: Registry integrity incident, self-reported. Two sessions were appending to this file concurrently and both drew event ids from the same counter, so e023 and e024 were defined twice with different content. Worse, the de-duplication pass that caught this resolved collisions by keeping whichever line came first and silently discarding the other, which deleted two genuine records - including the prototype verdict - from the ledger. Repair: every surviving event keeps its content, the colliding entries were renumbered to fresh free ids (e026 for the verdict, e027 for the KEXINIT correction, e028 for my deployment record), and nothing was dropped. Prevention recorded in FORMAT.md: a collision must abort the write, never resolve itself, and every write must be verified by unique-id count.

summary: Scale limits supplied by the user, answering Q7 and closing it: at most 50 devices (hosts), no single file larger than 100 MB, and total R2 usage must stay at or below 10 GB. The 100 MB per-file figure agrees with what event e014 already recorded ("single-file maximum size generally under 100 MB"), so that part is a confirmation rather than a change. The 10 GB ceiling is NEW and is a CAPACITY BUDGET, not merely a size limit: it implies the store must bound its own total bytes, which in turn requires a retention/eviction policy and a decision about whether superseded object versions stay in R2. Nothing in the schema or the code measures or enforces total stored bytes today. The 50-host figure bounds a full sweep and therefore the run/resume design, because D13 caps a single Cron invocation at 15 minutes of wall clock.

Grill round 4 answers. Q1 ACCEPTED: a cron sweep that works within a wall-clock budget and persists a cursor (which host, which path) into D1, resuming on the next invocation, with a target freshness of 15-30 minutes. Q2 REVISED BY THE USER, overriding the recommendation: old files are to be deleted automatically to stay inside the 10 GB budget, but files carrying an IMPORTANT mark are never deleted, and if the important-marked set alone fills the budget then no new files are synchronised at all. This introduces a requirement that did not exist before - a per-object importance/pin flag plus an eviction policy that must never delete a pinned object, and a capacity guard that refuses new work rather than evicting pins. Note the old policy of never deleting anything is now explicitly rejected. Q4 ACCEPTED: two tables, collection_runs plus collection_issues, to hold receipts including capacity refusals, which only become visible if they are persisted. Q3 PARTIALLY ANSWERED BUT CONFLICTS WITH A VERIFIED PLATFORM FACT: the user asked for a custom domain to serve presigned downloads with a 2-hour expiry and an optional share password, and D11 (research section 9.2, citing https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/) states that presigned URLs work only on <ACCOUNT_ID>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com and CANNOT be used with custom domains, the documented alternative being a public bucket behind WAF HMAC validation (Pro plan or above). The requirement as stated is achievable, but only by the Worker issuing its own short-lived signed token and streaming the object, not by an R2 presigned URL. That reinterpretation is PROPOSED, not yet confirmed by the user. Also recorded: the user pasted a root password into the conversation for the test host (identified dashboard-side, deliberately not written here); the repository is public, so the credential is deliberately NOT written anywhere in the repository and should be rotated after the experiment.

D28 was half wrong and is corrected. It asserted that Cloudflare provides NO CLI or API path for connecting a repository to a Worker, so the connection had to be a human-only dashboard step. That is false: Cloudflare documents a Workers Builds REST API (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/api-reference/, updated 2026-09-22) whose from-scratch example creates the repository connection (PUT /accounts/{id}/builds/repos/connections) and the production and preview triggers (POST /accounts/{id}/builds/triggers) entirely by API. What remains genuinely human-only is narrower and different: the one-time installation and authorization of the Cloudflare GitHub App, which requires an OAuth grant on the GitHub side. The documentation states this explicitly - once that one-time setup is done, the API can do everything else. Credential requirement, measured rather than assumed: the API needs a USER-scoped API token with the Workers Builds Configuration: Edit permission, and the existing wrangler OAuth token is NOT sufficient - GET /accounts/{id}/builds/tokens and GET /builds/repos/connections both returned 403 code 10000 Authentication error on 2026-10-07, while GET /accounts/{id}/workers/scripts succeeded with the same token, which isolates the failure to the Builds permission rather than to authentication in general. Recorded so no future session repeats the claim that the dashboard is the only path, and so the real prerequisite (GitHub App authorization) is not confused with the one that was wrongly claimed.
